implementation_notes: The C++17 baseline: std::optional is the context and a hand-written lift2 (or a variadic zip) is the ap, so the payload type is resolved at the call site by template deduction and no abstraction library is needed. Choose this whenever the toolchain is pre-C++23 or the team does not want a functional dependency; the cost is one helper per context and the loss of the failure reason, which optional does not model.
pitfalls: Dereferencing a disengaged optional is undefined behaviour: test both arguments before invoking the function.
optional has no error channel, so accumulation of distinct failures is impossible without changing the context.

variants.name: std::expected with and_then/transform and a container error type
variants.idiom_name: std::expected<T, E> and_then/transform + merged error container
variants.implementation_notes: The C++23 realization: std::expected<T, E> is the context and its monadic operations (and_then, transform, or_else, transform_error) supply the chaining, while combination stays explicit - each independent computation is evaluated, then the successes are fed to the combining function and the errors are merged into a container error type (typically std::vector<Error> or a fixed-capacity list). Choose it when the toolchain is C++23 and the failure reason must survive; it is the only standard-library option that can accumulate when the error type is a monoid rather than a single value.
pitfalls: expected propagates only the first error through and_then, so accumulation must happen in the combining expression (concatenating the error containers), not in the chain.
Choosing std::vector as the error type allocates on every merge; a small fixed-capacity error list avoids heap traffic on the failure path.
transform_error only maps the error, it does not merge two of them: teams routinely expect it to accumulate and get silent last-writer-wins.
